content.description: A 193-kilometer water corridor carries 12% of world trade. One ship ran aground in 2021 and stalled the planet: welcome to **Suez**.

hero.hook: 193 kilometers of canal, 12% of world trade: this is the story of the most strategic passage on earth.

blocks.text: On the morning of **March 23, 2021**, a sandstorm blows across northern Egypt. A giant container ship loses its heading. The photo below is taken four days later, from the International Space Station.

blocks.caption: Fields on the left, desert on the right. The blue strip in the middle is the Suez Canal.

stops.text: Fields on the left, desert on the right. The blue strip in the middle is the Suez Canal.
**The ship.** It is called the *Ever Given*. It is 400 m long, as long as the Empire State Building is tall. The canal here is about 300 m wide.
**The bow.** It has dug itself into the eastern bank. The stern is aground on the other side. Nothing can get past.
For six days, one of the busiest waterways in the world is shut by a single ship.

blocks.caption: Two radar images of the canal's southern entrance, four days apart. Every bright dot on the water is a ship.

stops.text: Two radar images of the canal's southern entrance, four days apart. Every bright dot on the water is a ship.
**March 21.** A normal day. A few dozen ships wait their turn.
**March 25.** The dots multiply. In the end about 400 ships are stuck, carrying oil, cars, furniture, even live animals.

blocks.text: Each day of blockage holds up goods worth more than 9 billion dollars. How did the world come to depend on a strip of water this narrow?

steps.text: A container leaves **Asia** for **Europe**. There are two ways to get there by sea.
**The long way**: all around Africa, past the Cape of Good Hope. For centuries, it was the only one.
**The shortcut**: through Egypt. It saves about 7,000 km and more than a week at sea.
The canal is 193 km of water dug through the desert, between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea. It has no locks: both seas are at the same level.

blocks.text: The canal opens in **1869**, after ten years of digging. The project is French, led by the diplomat Ferdinand de Lesseps. The work is Egyptian: tens of thousands of peasants are forced to dig, and many die.

blocks.caption: 1869: the first ships pass through, in a newspaper engraving of the time.

blocks.text: Egypt, deep in debt, soon sells its share to Britain. For the British Empire, the canal is the road to India. Its soldiers will guard it for more than seventy years.
In **July 1956**, Egypt's president, Gamal Abdel Nasser, announces that Egypt is taking the canal back. He will [[nationalize]] it and use its income to build a giant dam on the Nile.

blocks.caption: Cairo, August 1956. Nasser is cheered by the crowd a few days after his announcement.

blocks.explanation: The three countries invade in October 1956. But the United States and the Soviet Union both order them to stop. They withdraw, humiliated. The canal stays Egyptian.
options: They accept, and negotiate a price.
They attack Egypt, together with Israel.
blocks.text: How do Britain and France **react**? The three countries invade in October 1956. But the United States and the Soviet Union both order them to stop. They withdraw, humiliated. The canal stays Egyptian.

In 1967, a war between Israel and Egypt shut the canal for eight years. Fifteen cargo ships were trapped inside the whole time. Desert sand slowly covered their decks, and sailors nicknamed them the “Yellow Fleet.”
Today, about **12%** of world trade passes through the canal: some 50 ships a day in a normal year. For Egypt, the tolls are worth more than 9 billion dollars a year.

blocks.caption: The canal seen from a cargo ship. Vessels travel in convoys, one behind the other.

blocks.text: A passage like this has a name: a [[chokepoint]]. Everything depends on it staying open. And it does not take a ship turned sideways to close it.

steps.text: To reach the canal from Asia, ships must first pass a narrow strait at the bottom of the Red Sea: **Bab el-Mandeb**.
From **late 2023**, armed groups in Yemen attack cargo ships there with missiles and drones.
Many shipping companies give up on the shortcut. They send their ships the long way again, around Africa. In 2024, traffic through the canal falls by about half.

The Suez Canal is the shortest sea route between Asia and Europe. It saves about 7,000 km.
About 12% of world trade depends on it, which makes it a target and a prize: 1956, 1967, 2023.
One ship, one storm or one conflict is enough to send global trade the long way around.

1956.explanation: When Nasser nationalized the canal, France, Great Britain, and Israel invaded Egypt. Under American pressure (Eisenhower threatened to collapse the pound sterling), they had to withdraw - marking the end of Franco-British colonial power.

Bab-el-Mandeb.explanation: Strait located at the south of the Red Sea, between Yemen and Djibouti, constituting the mandatory crossing point to access the Suez Canal from the Indian Ocean.

Cape of Good Hope.explanation: A point located at the southern tip of Africa. Before the Suez Canal, ships had to bypass it to travel between Europe and Asia.

Ever Given.explanation: A 400m container ship that ran aground across the canal for 6 days, blocking 400 ships. It cost the world economy 400 million dollars per hour, perfectly illustrating the strategic importance of the canal in global chains.
